title: "Fitting a linear regression"

  enabled: true

The [Provo measurements](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) define each response as a mean log first fixation duration aggregated across readers and modeled cloze surprisal as the negative base 2 logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. The regression specifies a straight conditional mean for those summaries. We now need an estimation rule. **Ordinary least squares (OLS)** chooses the coefficients whose fitted values minimize the residual sum of squares. This is the squared error rule introduced for the observed sample; the [maximum likelihood connection](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) comes after the minimizer is derived.

Here a [**residual**](residuals.qmd) provisionally means $y_i-\widehat y_i$, the observed response minus its fitted value. The Gaussian likelihood factors over rows only under the stated [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption, and its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) controls the scale of squared error.

We first derive the squared error objective and its minimizer, then compute the Provo estimate and reconnect the resulting rule to its sampling assumptions.

The basic idea is to try a line, measure every vertical discrepancy, and then adjust the line until the sum of the squared discrepancies cannot be made smaller. Squaring serves two purposes in this calculation: it prevents a positive discrepancy $e$ and a negative discrepancy $-e$ from canceling, and it gives a larger discrepancy more weight. Their combined squared contribution is $e^2+(-e)^2=2e^2$.

## From discrepancies to an objective

For candidate coefficients $b_0$ and $b_1$, define

$$
\widetilde y_i(b_0,b_1)=b_0+b_1x_i
$$

and

$$
e_i(b_0,b_1)=y_i-\widetilde y_i(b_0,b_1).
$$

The OLS objective is

$$
Q(b_0,b_1)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i\right)^2.
$$

We use $b_0$ and $b_1$ while considering arbitrary candidate lines, then place hats on $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ for the candidates that minimize $Q$. This notation lets us distinguish the values being tried from the estimates selected by the rule.

We now use a [derivative](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change), which measures how a quantity changes under a very small change in its input. Here a partial derivative changes one coefficient while holding the other fixed. A positive derivative says that increasing that coefficient raises squared error locally; a negative derivative says that increasing it lowers squared error locally. Differentiate one coefficient at a time:

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_0}
=-2\sum_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i),
$$

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_1}
=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i).
$$

At the minimizer both derivatives are zero. The equations obtained by setting
these derivatives to zero are called the **normal equations**. The first normal
equation gives

$$
\sum_i y_i=n\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1\sum_i x_i,
$$

so

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\overline y-\widehat\beta_1\overline x.
$$

Substitute this expression into the second normal equation:

$$
0
=
\sum_i x_i
\left[
(y_i-\overline y)
-\widehat\beta_1(x_i-\overline x)
\right].
$$

Because the centered terms sum to zero, this is equivalent to

$$
\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)
=
\widehat\beta_1
\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2.
$$

Thus

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2}
$$

This formula requires at least two distinct observed predictor values, so that
$\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2>0$. Under that condition the squared error objective
curves upward in every coefficient direction. The solution at which both
derivatives equal zero is therefore the unique minimum rather than a maximum or
a flat region.

Before sampling, $\widehat\beta_1(\mathbf Y)$ is an estimator: a random function of the response vector. Once the observed vector $\mathbf y$ is inserted, $\widehat\beta_1(\mathbf y)$ is the numerical estimate printed below. The distinction follows the [estimator terminology](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd).

## Computing the Provo regression estimate

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-ols-by-hand
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
x <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
x_bar <- mean(x)
y_bar <- mean(y)
centered_cross_product <- sum((x - x_bar) * (y - y_bar))
centered_x_squares <- sum((x - x_bar)^2)

slope_by_hand <- centered_cross_product / centered_x_squares
intercept_by_hand <- y_bar - slope_by_hand * x_bar

provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- x
fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)

stopifnot(
  abs(slope_by_hand - coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_bits"]]) < 1e-12,
  abs(intercept_by_hand - coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]]) < 1e-12
)

observed_ols_calculation <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "number of Provo positions",
    "mean modeled cloze surprisal",
    "mean log first fixation duration",
    "centered x-y cross-product",
    "centered x sum of squares"
  ),
  observed_value = c(
    length(x),
    x_bar,
    y_bar,
    centered_cross_product,
    centered_x_squares
  )
)
observed_ols_calculation

observed_ols_estimates <- data.frame(
  term = c("intercept", "modeled cloze surprisal"),
  estimate_by_hand = c(intercept_by_hand, slope_by_hand),
  estimate_from_lm = unname(coef(fit))
)
observed_ols_estimates
```

The first table shows every observed quantity needed by the formulas. Substituting
those Provo values gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_1
&=
\frac{
`r format(centered_cross_product, digits = 7)`
}{
`r format(centered_x_squares, digits = 7)`
} \\
&=
`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`,
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_0
&=
`r format(y_bar, digits = 7)`
-
\left(`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`\right)
\left(`r format(x_bar, digits = 7)`\right) \\
&=
`r format(intercept_by_hand, digits = 7)`.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the directly calculated fitted line is

$$
\widehat m(x)
=
`r format(intercept_by_hand, digits = 7)`
+
`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`x.
$$

The second table checks these direct calculations against `lm()`. The two
methods agree to numerical precision, but the formulas, rather than the software
call, define the OLS estimate.

## Fitting the same line with `lm()`

The call used above was

```{r}
#| label: show-provo-lm-summary
fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)
summary(fit)
```

Read the formula from left to right. `mean_log_ffd` is the response. The tilde
means “is modeled using,” and `cloze_surprisal_bits` is the predictor. The
`data` argument tells R where those two columns are stored.

The printed output contains several summaries, each of which answers a different
question:

1. `Call` repeats the model specification that R fit.
2. `Residuals` reports selected quantiles of the [residuals](residuals.qmd), the
   observed responses minus their fitted values.
3. In `Coefficients`, `Estimate` contains the same intercept and slope calculated
   above. `Std. Error` describes sampling variation in each coefficient estimate,
   while the [coefficient $t$ statistic](regression-t-statistic.qmd) divides the
   distance from a stated null value by that standard error.
4. [Residual spread](residuals.qmd#residual-standard-error) estimates the
   conditional response variation around the line and explains the units and
   denominator of `Residual standard error`.
5. [$R^2$](coefficient-of-determination.qmd) compares the line's squared error
   with the squared error from predicting every response by the sample mean.
6. The [regression $F$ statistic](regression-f-statistic.qmd) compares that
   reduction in squared error with the residual spread.

The output gathers several quantities, each with its own interpretation and
sampling assumptions. At this point, we have derived only the two `Estimate`
entries. Each remaining quantity requires the additional assumptions stated in
its linked derivation.

The fitted slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_by_hand)`: one additional bit of modeled cloze surprisal corresponds to that change in the fitted word position mean of log first fixation duration. Squaring makes large vertical discrepancies count more heavily, which is one reason a few unusual responses may affect the fit.

Squared error is plausible when positive and negative deviations on the modeled scale should receive the same penalty and larger deviations should matter increasingly. This criterion comes from a working modeling decision rather than from the eye movement measurement itself. A heavy-tailed response model or absolute loss would reduce the relative influence of unusually large discrepancies.

If

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2),
$$

then the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
=
-n\log\sigma
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2
+C.
$$

For fixed $\sigma$, maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the
**error sum of squares (SSE)**. OLS and Gaussian maximum likelihood thus select
the same coefficient estimates.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-ols-fit
#| fig-cap: "Reader-aggregated Provo positions and the OLS conditional mean."
plot_data <- provo
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 160L)
)
grid$fitted <- intercept_by_hand +
  slope_by_hand * grid$cloze_surprisal_bits

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(plot_data, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

OLS supplies the best line under the squared error criterion. The adequacy of
that line and the dependence among passages remain open questions, which we
address through uncertainty calculations and diagnostics.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which quantity does OLS minimize?
2. Why does the slope contain cross-products of centered $x$ and $y$?
3. Under which response model does OLS coincide with maximum likelihood?
4. What feature of squared error makes influence worth checking later?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. OLS minimizes the residual sum of squares, $\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The centered cross-products measure whether deviations in $x$ and $y$ have the same direction; dividing by centered $x$ variation converts that co-movement into change in $y$ per unit $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. OLS coefficient estimates coincide with maximum likelihood under independent normal responses with linear means and a common variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Squaring gives unusually large residuals disproportionate weight, so a few observations can strongly affect the fitted coefficients. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next work through the [residuals](residuals.qmd) that remain after fitting the line.
